title: Vomiting and fast breathing in a 16-year-old student
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 16-year-old student in the ED with severe nausea and vomiting. She thinks it is gastro, but she has had 3 weeks of thirst, frequent urination, hunger and weight loss, and a family history of autoimmune disease. The candidate then interprets her observations, bloods and venous gas, urinalysis and ECG, diagnoses severe diabetic ketoacidosis, outlines management in the ED following the RCH guideline, explains the diagnosis to her and sets cerebral oedema escalation triggers.
focus: Vomiting in an adolescent: recognising diabetic ketoacidosis as the first presentation of type 1 diabetes, grading its severity and starting safe fluid, potassium and insulin management
stem: You are a junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital in NSW. Evelyn Marrow, a 16-year-old student, has come in with severe nausea and vomiting. She has been triaged, and her mother is in the waiting room. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from Evelyn and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results and venous blood gas, a urinalysis and an ECG. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting, and answer the examiner's questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Evelyn Marrow, a 16-year-old school student. You lie on the trolley with a vomit bowl beside you. You look pale and tired and you breathe deeply and quickly the whole time, but you are alert and answer sensibly. Your mum brought you in and is in the waiting room; you are happy to talk on your own. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I just can't stop throwing up. I think I've got gastro."

The vomiting (give only when asked)

  • You have felt sick since yesterday.
  • You have vomited about 6 times in the last 6 hours. You can't keep any food or drink down.
  • At first it was food. Now it is only small amounts of yellow fluid. There has been no blood.
  • At first about a cup each time, now only a few teaspoons.

Other symptoms (only when asked about each; if asked a vague "anything else?", say "Like what?")

  • Tummy: a mild soreness all over, 1 out of 10. It doesn't move anywhere and isn't worse in any one spot.
  • Breathing: "I feel short of breath, like I can't get enough air."
  • Weeing: for about 3 weeks you have been weeing much more than usual, about 10 times a day, and getting up 2 or 3 times a night to wee.
  • Thirst: for 3 weeks you have been really thirsty and drinking much more than usual.
  • Hunger: for 3 weeks you have been hungrier than usual and eating more.
  • Weight: your clothes are looser than they were a month ago. You haven't weighed yourself.

Negatives (only if asked about each)

  • No diarrhoea or constipation; your bowels are normal and you are passing wind. No blood or mucus in your poo. Nobody at home is sick.
  • No fever, shivers or chills.
  • No pain or burning when you wee, no blood in it, no change in your urine apart from going more often. No back or side pain.
  • No yellow skin or eyes, no dark urine. No pain in the upper tummy going through to your back.
  • No pain that started around the belly button and moved to the right side.
  • No headache, no problems with your vision, no dizziness or spinning, no light sensitivity. You have not been confused or drowsy.
  • No cough or sore throat.
  • No darkening of your skin and no craving for salt.
  • Periods: regular; your last period was 2 weeks ago and was normal. You are not sexually active, so you are sure you are not pregnant.

Past history, medicines and allergies

  • Previously healthy. No operations and no hospital admissions. Immunisations up to date.
  • No medicines, no contraception, no supplements. No recreational drugs.
  • No known allergies.

Family history (only when asked)

  • Your mother has Graves' disease (an overactive thyroid).
  • Your father has coeliac disease.
  • No one in the family has diabetes that you know of.

Social history

  • You are a school student. You can't go to school while you are this sick.
  • You live with your parents and feel well supported at home.
  • You don't smoke or drink alcohol. No overseas travel.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Idea: "I think I've got gastro."
  • Concern: you are worried because you can't eat or drink anything.
  • Expectation: "I just want to stop feeling so unwell, doctor."

The nurse and how Evelyn changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the triage set: RR 26 (deep breaths), SpO2 99% on room air, BP 108/68, HR 126 regular, temperature 36.9 °C, alert, pain 1/10.
  • If the candidate asks for a finger-prick blood glucose, the nurse says: "The meter just reads HI." If asked for capillary ketones: "A blood ketone level went off with the bloods; it will come with the other results."
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "She's just vomited again, only a few teaspoons of yellow fluid."
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic, the nurse gives it and Evelyn says she feels a little less sick. Her breathing stays deep and fast whatever is done in Part 1.
  • If the candidate orders IV fluids, the nurse says she will set them up, and the examiner says: "Noted. Please cover your management in Part 2."
  • If the candidate orders insulin in Part 1, the nurse asks: "Do you want to wait for the potassium and get the fluids going first?"
  • If the candidate asks for bloods, a gas, a urine test or an ECG, the examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: thin, pale and unwell, tired but alert, GCS 15. Deep, rapid, sighing breathing. A sweet, fruity (acetone) smell on her breath. Height 165 cm, weight 52 kg (BMI 19).
  • Hydration: Dry lips and mucous membranes, sunken eyes. CRT 2 seconds, warm hands and feet, strong peripheral pulses. JVP 1 cm above the sternal angle.
  • Skin, neck and eyes: no rash, no pigmentation of skin creases or inside the mouth. No goitre, no eye signs of thyroid disease. No jaundice.
  • Chest: equal expansion, resonant, clear breath sounds throughout, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Heart: tachycardic, dual heart sounds, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen: not distended, soft and non-tender, no guarding or rebound, no masses, liver and spleen not palpable, bowel sounds present. Renal angles not tender. Hernial orifices normal.
  • Neurological: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no neck stiffness, no focal deficit. Fundi normal if examined.
  • Ears and throat: normal.
  • Pelvic or rectal examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms Evelyn's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Asks the sensitive questions (sexual activity, drugs, alcohol) while she is on her own, explaining confidentiality and its limits, and offers to involve her mother.
Acknowledges how unwell she feels and her worry about not keeping fluids down, uses plain language and explains each part of the examination.
check.d: Credit an early antiemetic order here.

check.x: History
Characterises the vomiting:

kids.x: Onset and frequency: nausea since yesterday, about 6 vomits in the last 6 hours
Content: food at first, now yellow fluid; asks specifically about blood (none)
Volume and intake: a cup at first, now teaspoons; cannot keep food or drink down

check.x: Asks about abdominal pain: mild, diffuse soreness at 1/10, no localising or migrating pain.
Elicits the hyperglycaemia symptom cluster over 3 weeks:

kids.x: Polyuria: weeing about 10 times a day, with nocturia
Weight loss: clothes looser than a month ago

check.x: Asks about breathing and elicits shortness of breath, and screens for cough or chest symptoms.
Uses cluster questions to screen other causes of vomiting (credit each cluster covered):

kids.x: Gastroenteritis and obstruction: diarrhoea, sick contacts, bowels opening and passing wind, previous surgery
Inflammatory and surgical causes: blood or mucus in stool (IBD), migrating right iliac fossa pain (appendicitis), jaundice, RUQ or epigastric pain to the back (hepatitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis)
Infection: fever, rigors or chills, dysuria, loin pain (pyelonephritis)
Neurological: headache, visual change, drowsiness (raised intracranial pressure), photophobia (migraine), vertigo (vestibular)
Endocrine: skin darkening, salt craving, faintness (Addison's disease)

check.x: Asks about pregnancy: last menstrual period (2 weeks ago), sexual activity (not active) and contraception.
Takes the past history: previously well, no surgery or admissions, immunisations up to date.
Takes a medication history: no medicines, contraception, supplements or recreational drugs; no known drug allergies.
Asks about family history of diabetes and autoimmune disease and elicits mother with Graves' disease and father with coeliac disease.
Takes the social history: student missing school, lives with parents, well supported, no smoking or alcohol, no travel.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is gastro, worried she cannot eat or drink, wants to stop feeling unwell.
Examination
General inspection: notes she is thin and unwell with deep, rapid, sighing (Kussmaul) breathing and a fruity, ketotic smell on the breath.
check.d: Credit naming the breathing pattern in plain words (deep, fast breathing).

check.x: Asks for the full set of observations including conscious state and identifies the tachycardia (HR 126) and tachypnoea (RR 26).
Asks for a bedside capillary blood glucose (and ketones) during Part 1 and recognises that a reading of HI means marked hyperglycaemia.
Assesses hydration: mucous membranes, CRT and peripheral perfusion, JVP, and estimates her as significantly dehydrated.
Examines the abdomen for tenderness, peritonism and masses, bowel sounds and renal angles (soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present).
Examines the chest for a precipitating infection and records a baseline neurological assessment (GCS, pupils).
Interpretation

Identifies RR 26 to 28 and HR 126 to 128 as yellow-zone values needing review; recognises the fast breathing as compensation for acidosis (SpO2 99%) and that perfusion is maintained (CRT 2 s, warm, normal BP), so she is not shocked.
Interprets the venous gas as a severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, HCO3 4) with appropriate respiratory compensation (pCO2 15) and a raised anion gap of 26, with a normal lactate.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: Winter's formula (expected pCO2 1.5 × 4 + 8 = 14 ± 2).

check.x: States that glucose 38.2, venous pH below 7.3 and blood ketones 6.0 (urine ketones ++) meet the criteria for DKA, and grades it as severe because the pH is below 7.1 (and the bicarbonate below 5).

Interprets the electrolytes: K 5.3 despite a total body potassium deficit, which will fall once insulin starts; the low measured sodium is from hyperglycaemia (corrected about 143) (accept corrected Na 140 to 145, depending on the formula); raised urea and creatinine are prerenal from dehydration.
Recognises no evidence of infection (WCC often raised in DKA; afebrile, CRP 3, clean urine) and a negative pregnancy test.
check.d: Credit normal lipase and LFTs, and osmolality 310 below the HHS range.

check.x: Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with no peaked T waves or U waves, a baseline for potassium shifts.

Gives severe diabetic ketoacidosis as the first presentation of type 1 diabetes, justified by at least 3 of: 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath, the autoimmune family history, and the results (glucose 38.2, pH 7.05, blood ketones 6.0).

Gives at least 2 differentials, each with a feature for or against it from this case (for example gastroenteritis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, sepsis or pyelonephritis, pregnancy or hyperemesis, adrenal crisis).
Management
Calls for senior help and involves the paediatric or endocrinology team early; assesses using DRSABCD/ABCDE, inserts 2 IV cannulae, and discusses HDU or ICU because the DKA is severe.

Gives a 0.9% sodium chloride bolus of 10 mL/kg (about 520 mL) and reassesses, keeping 20 mL/kg for shock. Then replaces the remaining deficit plus maintenance slowly over about 48 hours, without repeated or aggressive boluses.
Adds potassium to the rehydration fluid (40 mmol/L) once the potassium is known to be below 5.5 mmol/L and she is passing urine, with cardiac monitoring.

Starts an IV insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour (about 2.6 to 5.2 units/hour) after fluids have been running for about an hour and the potassium is known, with no insulin bolus and no bicarbonate.
Adds glucose (5%) to the fluids when the blood glucose falls below about 15 mmol/L, and continues insulin until the ketoacidosis resolves.
Monitors hourly blood glucose, vital signs, neurological observations and fluid balance, and checks ketones, electrolytes (including corrected sodium) and a venous gas every 1 to 2 hours.

Plans the follow-on care: looks for a precipitant; once she is stable sends islet autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2), coeliac serology and thyroid function; refers to the diabetes team for education and subcutaneous insulin.
Safety netting

Asks the nurses to escalate urgently for warning signs of cerebral oedema: at least 3 of headache, irritability or confusion, falling GCS, recurrent vomiting, slowing heart rate, rising BP, pupil changes.
check.d: Credit a rapid response for any red-zone observation and having mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV or 3% sodium chloride 2.5 to 5 mL/kg IV ready.

check.x: Explains in plain words that this is not gastro but diabetes (her body has stopped making insulin), that she needs a drip and insulin in hospital, that nothing she did caused it and it is lifelong but manageable, and checks her understanding.
check.d: Credit saying the diabetes team will teach her and her family, offering to bring her mother in, and telling Evelyn to report headache, confusion, drowsiness, more vomiting or worse breathing at once.

part2.lead: Here are Evelyn's observations, her blood results and venous gas, her urinalysis and her ECG.
part2.patient:
Question 4 opens with Evelyn's own question. React to the answer:

  • If told it is diabetes, look shocked: "So it's not gastro? Is it because I ate too much junk food?" Accept a kind explanation that nothing she did caused it.
  • If the candidate uses jargon (ketoacidosis, type 1, infusion), ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. Triage set at 14:10 and the nurse's repeat set at 14:40 at cannulation. Finger-prick glucose meter reads HI. Charted on the adult Between the Flags (SAGO) chart, used from age 16.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: if IV fluids were ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate they are being set up at 14:40.
  • Read: RR 26 rising to 28 (yellow zone), HR 126 rising to 128 (yellow zone). BP 108/68 then 104/66, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 then 36.8 °C and alert are all white. Glucose meter reads HI (above its range).
  • Meaning: deep, fast breathing with a normal SpO2 is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a lung problem. The tachycardia reflects significant dehydration. Perfusion is maintained (CRT 2 s, warm peripheries, normal BP, lactate 1.6), so she is dehydrated but not shocked; hypotension is a late sign, so BP alone cannot exclude shock. She is afebrile.
  • Changes: yellow-zone values call for a clinical review (this review) and closer observations; with a glucose of HI and her clinical state a senior should review her now. Call a rapid response for any red-zone value or a fall in conscious state.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2: vomiting, unable to keep fluids down, breathing fast. BGL meter reads HI.
Vomited a few teaspoons of yellow fluid. IV cannula inserted, bloods and VBG sent.

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Evelyn Marrow, UR 987654. Collected 14:40 at cannulation; venous gas on room air at the same time. Sample not haemolysed. No previous results on file.
handover.model:
• Read: glucose 38.2 and beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.0. pH 7.05, HCO3 4, BE −24, pCO2 15, lactate normal. Calculated anion gap 131 − (101 + 4) = 26. Na 131, K 5.3, urea 9.8, creatinine 98, calculated osmolality 310. WCC 14.2 with neutrophilia, haematocrit 0.48, CRP 3. Lipase and LFTs normal.
  • Meaning: high glucose, acidosis and ketonaemia meet the criteria for DKA, and a pH below 7.1 with a bicarbonate below 5 makes it severe. The acidosis has a raised anion gap from ketones, not lactate, and is appropriately compensated (Winter's: expected pCO2 1.5 × 4 + 8 = 14 ± 2). Winter's formula is derived for arterial gases; on a venous sample this is an approximate check, and a venous pCO2 of 15 still indicates maximal appropriate compensation. K 5.3 hides a total body deficit: insulin will drive potassium into cells and it will fall fast. Measured sodium is low because glucose draws water out of cells; corrected sodium is about 143. Urea, creatinine and haematocrit show dehydration. WCC is often raised in DKA; with a normal CRP and no fever it does not mean infection. Osmolality 310 is below the HHS range. Normal lipase and LFTs make pancreatitis and hepatobiliary causes unlikely.
  • Changes: treat as severe DKA following the RCH guideline: 10 mL/kg saline, potassium in the fluids because K is below 5.5, insulin infusion after the first hour, then repeat glucose hourly and electrolytes, ketones and gas every 1 to 2 hours. Watch that the corrected sodium rises as glucose falls.

handover.label: Urinalysis
handover.result: Midstream urine, 14:50. Bedside dipstick and pregnancy test; sample sent to the laboratory for microscopy (reported 15:40) and culture. Culture to follow.
handover.model:
• Read: glucose 4+ and ketones 2+. No leucocytes, nitrites or blood; microscopy shows no white cells or bacteria. Urine pregnancy test negative.
  • Meaning: glycosuria and ketonuria fit DKA (the blood ketone result is the more reliable measure). No evidence of a urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis as a precipitant. She is not pregnant, so hyperemesis is excluded.
  • Changes: follow up the culture; use blood ketones, not urine ketones, to monitor treatment.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result: 12-lead ECG, 14:45. Sinus tachycardia, rate 128/min, regular. Normal axis. PR 140 ms. QRS 80 ms. QTc 430 ms. Normal T wave morphology with no peaked T waves. No U waves. No ST elevation or depression. No previous ECG for comparison.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 128/min with normal intervals and axis; no peaked T waves, no U waves, no ST changes.
  • Meaning: the tachycardia fits dehydration and acidosis. No ECG sign of hyperkalaemia now, and this is a baseline for the fall in potassium expected once insulin starts.
  • Changes: continuous cardiac monitoring while potassium and insulin are running; repeat the ECG if potassium falls low or rises high.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Evelyn Marrow, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Evelyn now, here in the emergency department.
Evelyn asks you, "So is it just gastro? Why do I need a drip?" Please answer her, then tell me what you would ask the nurses to watch for.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Evelyn Marrow, 16, UR 987654.
  • Situation: severe DKA, likely new-onset type 1 diabetes; requesting urgent review.
  • Background: 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss; vomiting 6 times in 6 hours, unable to keep fluids down; previously well; mother Graves', father coeliac.
  • Assessment: RR 28 and HR 128 (yellow zone), perfusion maintained (CRT 2 s, warm, normal BP), so not shocked, GCS 15; glucose 38.2, pH 7.05, HCO3 4, ketones 6.0 = severe DKA, appropriately compensated, AG 26; K 5.3 but total body deplete; corrected Na about 143; prerenal; no infection, hCG negative; ECG sinus tachycardia, no hyperkalaemic changes.
  • Recommendation: 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline started or being started now; please review now for the insulin and potassium plan and HDU or ICU.

Severe diabetic ketoacidosis, first presentation of type 1 diabetes: 3 weeks of osmotic symptoms and weight loss, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, autoimmune family history; glucose 38.2, pH 7.05, ketones 6.0.

  • Gastroenteritis: for: vomiting, her own belief; against: no diarrhoea, 3 weeks of symptoms, results.
  • Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: for: glucose 38.2; against: osmolality 310, marked ketoacidosis.
  • Sepsis or pyelonephritis (precipitant or mimic): for: tachycardia, WCC 14.2; against: afebrile, CRP 3, clean urine.
  • Pregnancy or hyperemesis: against: not sexually active, hCG negative.
  • Adrenal crisis: for: autoimmune family history, vomiting, low sodium; against: hyperglycaemia, no pigmentation, corrected sodium normal.

1. Call for help: senior ED, paediatric and endocrinology teams; DRSABCD, 2 IV cannulae, cardiac monitoring; discuss HDU or ICU (severe DKA).
  2. Fluids: 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg (about 520 mL), reassess (20 mL/kg only if shocked); then deficit plus maintenance over about 48 hours.
  3. Potassium: 40 mmol/L in the fluids since K is below 5.5, once passing urine.
  4. Insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h (2.6 to 5.2 units/h), started about 1 hour after fluids; no bolus, no bicarbonate.
  5. Add 5% glucose when BGL falls below about 15 mmol/L.
  6. Monitor: hourly BGL, observations, neurological observations and fluid balance; ketones, electrolytes and VBG every 1 to 2 hours.
  7. Find any precipitant; later: islet antibodies, coeliac serology, TFTs; diabetes team.

• Plain words: not gastro; her body has stopped making insulin (type 1 diabetes), so sugar and acids have built up and she is very dry. The drip replaces fluid and salts and the insulin clears the acid. Nothing she ate caused it. It is lifelong but manageable with insulin; the diabetes team will teach her and her family. Offers to bring her mother in and checks understanding.
  • Nurses: report at once headache, irritability or confusion, falling GCS, recurrent vomiting, slowing heart rate, rising BP or pupil changes (possible cerebral oedema); rapid response for any red-zone value; cerebral oedema treatment ready.

ddx.dx: Severe diabetic ketoacidosis as the first presentation of type 1 diabetes
ddx.for: Three weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss, then vomiting, Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath, an autoimmune family history, glucose 38.2, pH 7.05 and blood ketones 6.0.
Nausea and repeated vomiting, and she thinks it is gastro.
ddx.against: No diarrhoea or sick contacts, 3 weeks of osmotic symptoms and weight loss, and a severe ketoacidosis with a glucose of 38.2.
Calculated osmolality is 310, she is alert, and she has marked ketonaemia with a pH of 7.05.

ddx.dx: Sepsis, such as pyelonephritis, as a precipitant or mimic
ddx.for: Tachycardia, vomiting and a WCC of 14.2 with neutrophilia.
ddx.against: Afebrile, no rigors, dysuria or loin pain, CRP 3, and no leucocytes, nitrites or bacteria in the urine.

ddx.for: A young woman with severe vomiting and ketonuria.
ddx.against: Not sexually active, normal period 2 weeks ago, and a negative urine pregnancy test.

ddx.for: Strong autoimmune family history, vomiting, abdominal soreness, dehydration and a low measured sodium.
ddx.against: Glucose is high not low, the corrected sodium is normal, K is only 5.3, no pigmentation, and the ketoacidosis explains the picture.

guide:
In Part 1, Evelyn gives each detail only when asked. The 3-week history of thirst, urination, hunger and weight loss comes out only to specific questions, and if asked a vague "anything else?" she says "Like what?". The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If asked, the nurse gives the triage observations and says the glucose meter reads HI, and she reports the further vomit partway through. If the candidate orders treatment in Part 1, say "Noted, please cover it in Part 2", except an antiemetic, which the nurse gives (Evelyn feels a little less sick). If they order insulin before the fluids or potassium, the nurse prompts them. If they ask for bloods, a gas, urine or an ECG, say these come in Part 2. Evelyn's mother is in the waiting room, so the candidate can ask the sensitive questions with Evelyn alone.

In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, the urinalysis and the ECG, then ask all four questions in order. If fluids were ordered in Part 1, say they are being set up at 14:40. Read out Evelyn's question to open question 4; she asks her follow-up question while the candidate answers.

The hospital is in NSW and charts adult observations on the Between the Flags chart from age 16. The paediatric team follows the RCH/ISPAD-based DKA protocol, so this station follows the RCH (paediatric) DKA guideline because Evelyn is 16. Some hospitals manage 16 and 17 year olds on an adult protocol. Credit a candidate who says they would follow local policy, but they should still give weight-based fluids and insulin and recognise the cerebral oedema risk.

A high-performing candidate finds the osmotic symptoms, weight loss and shortness of breath, and asks about pregnancy confidentially. They elicit the autoimmune family history and screen the other causes of vomiting by cluster. They notice the Kussmaul breathing and ketotic breath and ask for a finger-prick glucose in Part 1. In Part 2 they diagnose and grade severe DKA, recognise that potassium will fall with insulin, and correct the sodium. They give 10 mL/kg saline, potassium, an insulin infusion with no bolus after the first hour, and glucose once BGL is below 15. They monitor closely, escalate cerebral oedema signs and explain the diagnosis kindly.

A borderline candidate accepts "gastro", misses the 3-week history or the breathing, gives large fluid boluses or an insulin bolus, starts insulin without knowing the potassium, or forgets cerebral oedema.
explain:
Diagnosis: severe diabetic ketoacidosis, new-onset type 1 diabetes

Evelyn thinks she has gastro, but the history tells a different story. For 3 weeks she has had the classic symptoms of hyperglycaemia: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss. These were followed by nausea, vomiting, mild diffuse abdominal soreness and shortness of breath. The breathlessness is deep, sighing Kussmaul breathing, the respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, and her breath smells of ketones. Her parents have autoimmune diseases (Graves' disease and coeliac disease), which raises her risk of type 1 diabetes. Vomiting in a child or adolescent with a history like this is DKA until proven otherwise, and a bedside glucose should be checked early.

DKA is diagnosed from three features: hyperglycaemia (BGL above 11 mmol/L), acidosis (venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, ISPAD 2022) and ketosis (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3 mmol/L or more, or moderate to large urine ketones). Severity is graded by pH or bicarbonate: mild (pH below 7.3 or HCO3 below 18), moderate (pH below 7.2 or HCO3 below 10) and severe (pH below 7.1 or HCO3 below 5). Evelyn's pH of 7.05 makes her DKA severe, and her bicarbonate of 4 mmol/L, below 5, also meets the RCH severe threshold.

Taking the history

Use reading time to list the causes of vomiting in a teenager and screen each by cluster: gastrointestinal (gastroenteritis, obstruction, IBD, appendicitis, hepatobiliary disease, pancreatitis), infection (pyelonephritis), pregnancy and hyperemesis, neurological (raised intracranial pressure, migraine, vestibular causes) and endocrine (DKA, Addison's disease). Ask specifically about thirst, urination, appetite and weight, because adolescents rarely volunteer them. Take the sexual and substance history confidentially. Ask about family autoimmune disease.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and HR are in the yellow zone. The fast breathing is compensation, not lung disease (SpO2 99%). The tachycardia shows dehydration. Perfusion is maintained (CRT 2 s, warm peripheries, normal BP, lactate 1.6), so she is dehydrated but not shocked; hypotension is a late sign, so BP alone cannot exclude shock.
  • Gas: severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, HCO3 4) with a raised anion gap of 26 (131 − (101 + 4)) from ketones; the lactate is normal. The pCO2 of 15 is what Winter's formula predicts (1.5 × 4 + 8 = 14 ± 2), so compensation is appropriate. Winter's formula is derived for arterial gases; on a venous sample this is an approximate check, and a venous pCO2 of 15 still indicates maximal appropriate compensation. A bicarbonate below 5 also meets the RCH severe threshold.
  • Potassium: total body potassium is depleted by vomiting and osmotic diuresis. Acidosis and lack of insulin keep it in the blood, so the serum level looks normal or high. Insulin moves potassium into cells, and the level can drop fast.
  • Sodium: high glucose draws water out of cells and dilutes the sodium. Corrected sodium = measured Na + 2 × ((glucose − 5.6) ÷ 5.6), about 143 here (accept corrected Na 140 to 145, depending on the formula). As the glucose falls the corrected sodium should stay steady or rise; a falling corrected sodium is a warning sign for cerebral oedema.
  • Other bloods: raised urea, creatinine and haematocrit show dehydration. A raised WCC is common in DKA and does not on its own mean infection. Normal lipase and LFTs; osmolality 310 is below the range for HHS.
  • Urine: glycosuria and ketonuria, no infection, pregnancy test negative.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia without hyperkalaemic changes; a baseline for monitoring potassium.

The core first-line tests are BGL, blood ketones, a venous gas, UEC, FBC, an ECG and a urinalysis with MCS. A beta-hCG, CRP, lipase and LFTs help exclude differentials. Once she is stable, send islet autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2), coeliac serology and thyroid function, because autoimmune thyroid and coeliac disease are associated with type 1 diabetes.

Management (RCH Diabetic ketoacidosis guideline)

  • Call for help: senior ED, paediatric and endocrinology teams. Assess with DRSABCD, insert 2 IV cannulae and start cardiac monitoring. Severe DKA is discussed with ICU.
  • Fluids: a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (about 520 mL), then reassess. Give 20 mL/kg only if she is shocked. Then replace the remaining deficit plus maintenance evenly over about 48 hours. Repeated or aggressive boluses are avoided.
  • Potassium: add 40 mmol/L to the rehydration fluid once the potassium is known to be below 5.5 mmol/L and she is passing urine.
  • Insulin: an IV infusion of 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, started after IV fluids have been running for about an hour. No insulin bolus. Bicarbonate is not given.
  • Glucose: add 5% glucose to the fluids when the BGL falls below about 15 mmol/L, so insulin can continue to clear the ketones without causing hypoglycaemia.
  • Monitoring: hourly BGL, vital signs, neurological observations and strict fluid balance; ketones, electrolytes and a venous gas every 1 to 2 hours, with corrected sodium.
  • After resolution: once the acidosis has resolved and she is eating and drinking, move to subcutaneous insulin with the diabetes team, and give education for Evelyn and her family.

Some hospitals manage 16 and 17 year olds on an adult protocol (Therapeutic Guidelines). Follow local policy, but the risk of cerebral oedema in new-onset DKA in adolescents is why careful fluids and close neurological monitoring matter.

Cerebral oedema

This is the main cause of death in paediatric DKA. Risk factors are a new diagnosis, severe acidosis, a low pCO2, a high urea and bicarbonate treatment; Evelyn has several. Warning signs include headache, irritability or confusion, a falling GCS, recurrent vomiting, a slowing heart rate, rising BP and pupil changes. Treat at once: call for senior help, raise the head of the bed, reduce the fluid rate, and give mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV or 3% sodium chloride 2.5 to 5 mL/kg IV, then arrange ICU.

Differentials

Gastroenteritis is the common mistake; HHS is distinguished by a very high osmolality with little ketosis; sepsis or pyelonephritis may precipitate or mimic DKA; pregnancy is excluded by history and test; adrenal crisis is worth thinking of with her autoimmune family history but does not cause hyperglycaemia.

Safety netting and follow-up

Evelyn needs a plain-words explanation that this is type 1 diabetes, that nothing she did caused it and that it is lifelong but manageable. She and the nurses report headache, confusion, drowsiness, more vomiting or worse breathing at once. After discharge she is followed up by the diabetes clinic and her GP, with education on insulin, glucose and ketone monitoring and sick-day management.
points: Vomiting with polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and weight loss in a young person is DKA until proven otherwise; check a bedside glucose and ketones early.

DKA needs hyperglycaemia, acidosis (venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L) and ketosis (blood ketones 3 mmol/L or more); severity is graded by pH or bicarbonate, with pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 severe.
Serum potassium is often normal or high at presentation despite a total body deficit, and it falls fast with insulin; add potassium to the fluids once K is known to be below 5.5 mmol/L.

RCH management: a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus, the deficit replaced over about 48 hours, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour after the first hour with no bolus, and glucose added below about 15 mmol/L.
Cerebral oedema is the main danger in new-onset paediatric DKA: watch for headache, confusion, falling GCS, slowing heart rate and rising BP, and treat at once with mannitol or hypertonic saline.
Type 1 diabetes clusters with other autoimmune diseases; screen for coeliac and thyroid disease once she is stable.
